# 1.1 Population modeling background {.center}

## Structured populations

> Populations, i.e., collections of interacting organisms of the same
> species, have a variety of structures.

-   Sexes: female and male

-   Ages: newborn, yearlings, juveniles, adults

-   Spatial and dynamic

::: notes
Populations, have a variety of interesting structures. For example,
populations contain individuals of different ages ... sexes... and have
age-sex structured.

Another universal and fascinating characteristic of populations, which
is the focus of this course is that they have spatial structures.
meaning that we can always find more or fewer individuals in some areas
than in other areas, while sometimes we might find none at all.

On top of that, spatial structures are dynamic, meaning that they change
over time

An area with none of a species in a year may have a few individuals of
that species in the next year

The underlying processes are spatially structured population dynamics:
BIDE
:::

## Demography

$$\Delta N = B + I - D - E$$

Spatially structured population dynamics and underlying prcesses are
driven by heterogeneity and dynamics of abiotic, as well as intra- and
inter-specific interactions.

![](images/sifaka.GIF){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

::: notes
The processes underlying spatially structured population dynamics are
called BIDE

These are demographic and dispersal processes that determine changes in
population size

E and I are called dispersal movement or movement

READ then:

understanding spatially structured population dynamics has been very
challenging to ecologists, partly due to our inability to obtain
“complete” observations of populations at relevant spatial and temporal
scales.

For example, we might mistakenly think that an area was not used by a
skink species (or say the local population size of the skink was 0 for
that area) simply because the two little skinks living in that area
happened to be hiding under a rock when we were trying to find them
during the survey of the area. Or, we could be unsure if a sifaka was
dead or alive, and if it was alive, where it was, after we captured it
for the last time. Without complete observations about populations,
ecologists heavily rely on statistical models to estimate the
whereabouts, numbers, birth, death, and movement of organisms from
partial observations (i.e., data). Nowadays, these statistical models
become more and more complex to satisfy our curiosity about natural
populations and their complexity, making these models challenging to
build and compute.
:::

## Previously

> Metapopulation is defined as a set of connected local populations that
> persist in a balance between local extinctions and colonization.

The concept has been generalized to any spatially structured population
that inhabits heterogeneous habitats.

-   As oposed to classic metapopulation models, modern statistical
    models account for imperfect detection.

::: notes
If we look at the history of spatial population modeling, it roots back
into metapopulation models. While the concept of metapopulation tends to
be constrained to local populations that inhabit patchy habitats and
have a high rate of turnover (i.e., extinctioncolonization; Hanski and
Gilpin 1997, p. 9), later it has been generalized to any spatially
structured populations that can inhabit patchy to continuous habitats
(as long as the habitat is heterogeneous) and have any rate of turnover,
even including the situation without any turnover at all. Another
distinction between “classic” metapopulation models and “modern”
statistical models is that, while
:::

# 1.2 Occupancy framework {.center}

## Imperfect Detection

-   **Raw Observations vs Latent Reality**:
    -   $y_{ijt} = 0$ can mean **True Absence** ($z_{it} = 0$) OR
        **Non-Detection** ($z_{it} = 1, p < 1$).
    -   Naive raw proportion of occupied sites
        ($\hat{\psi}_{\text{naive}}$) severely underestimates true
        occupancy.
-   **False Negative Probability**: $(1 - p)^J$, where $J$ is the number
    of secondary visits.
-   **Biological Consequence**: Masking population declines, range
    contractions, and extinction events.

::: notes
How? by separating observations from the true ecological process in a
hierachical framework.

modern statistical models can be considered the generalized forms of
classic metapopulation models in terms of both their ecological realism
and statistical elegance.

Such generalization is undoubtedly thanks to the broad application of
Geographic Information System (GIS) and synthesis of metapopulation
ecology and landscape ecology (Howell et al. 2018; Royle et al. 2018).

Next, we will talk about the evolution of mathematical and statistical
models that have been developed and used to understand metapopulations
and more generally spatially structured populations over the last half
century.
:::

## Static Occupancy Model

-   **Process Sub-model**:
    $$z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i), \quad \text{logit}(\psi_i) = \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}$$
-   **Observation Sub-model**:
    $$y_{ij} | z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i p_{ij}), \quad \text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \mathbf{W}_{ij} \boldsymbol{\alpha}$$
-   **Assumptions**:
    1.  Closure: Occupancy state $z_i$ is constant across
        $j = 1, \dots, J$ visits.
    2.  Independence of detections conditional on $z_i$.
    3.  No false positives ($P(y=1 | z=0) = 0$).

::: notes
We talked about static occupancy models as a basic model with two
submodels.

Occupancy is probably the simplest way to measure population status and
thus provides limited information for the spatial structures and
dynamics of populations. Occupancy status, which is often represented by
1’s (presence) and 0’s (absence), is a reduced form of abundance in the
sense that the study species will be considered present at a site as
long as there is at least one individual of the species at that site
(i.e., local abundance ≥1), and absent only when there is no individual
at all at that site (i.e., local abundance = 0).
:::

## Dynamic Occupancy Model

-   **Initial State** ($t = 1$):
    $$z_{i,1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_{i,1})$$
-   **State Transitions** ($t > 1$):
    $$z_{i,t} | z_{i,t-1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left( z_{i,t-1} \phi_{i,t-1} + (1 - z_{i,t-1}) \gamma_{i,t-1} \right)$$
-   **Parameters**:
    -   $\psi_1$: Initial occupancy probability
    -   $\phi_{i,t-1}$: Persistence probability ($1 - \epsilon_{i,t-1}$)
    -   $\gamma_{i,t-1}$: Colonization probability
-   **Observation submodel** for primary period $t$ and secondary visit
    $j \in \{1, \dots, J_{i,t}\}$:
    $$y_{ijt} | z_{it} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_{it} p_{ijt})$$

::: notes
By specifying that occupancy status is only a function of environmental
conditions at the same time (although time is not specified in the model
and thus is only implied), the model basically assumes that species
occupancy always tracks environmental changes instantaneously (or there
is no environmental change at all). However, this is hardly the case in
reality, as the state of a population at a given time is arguably always
related to its status in the past, and it normally takes some time for a
population to respond to environmental changes. The dynamic occupancy
model (MacKenzie et al. 2003; Royle and Kéry 2007) deals with such an
issue by modeling changes in occupancy as a function of covariates,
rather than linking occupancy to covariates directly (except for the
first year). The dynamic occupancy model is a model for discrete time
steps (also called primary occasions), and these time steps in practice
are often years, or breeding seasons. But note that the time steps
necessary to describe occupancy dynamics in an adequate manner will have
to be adapted to the life-cycle of a study species: a time step may be 1
day for a metapopulation of some damselfly species or successive 10
years for a tree species.

Dynamic occupancy models (MacKenzie et al. 2003; Royle and Kéry 2007)
further explain the temporal changes of occupancy status with local
extinction (change from 1 to 0) and colonization (change from 0 to 1),
which again is a reduced form of the BIDE processes in the sense that a
local population goes extinct when all individuals at that site either
die (D) or emigrate (E) without giving birth (B) to any new individual,
and an unoccupied site is colonized when at least one individual
immigrates (I) into this site. Despite the limited information occupancy
models can provide, they are nonetheless one of the most broadly used
family of models in population ecology, due to the relative ease with
which detection/non-detection data can be collected.

The process sub-model first describes the initial occupancy status
(i.e., occupancy at the first year) using basically Eq. (2.1) for the
static occupancy model; however, now z, ψ and x’s are all indexed by 1
to indicate that they are for t = 1.

From the second year (i.e., t ≥ 2), the model assumes that a site that
is occupied in year t has a probability of remaining occupied in year
t + 1 (persistence, the opposite of extinction), and a site that is
unoccupied in year t has a probability to become occupied in year t + 1
(colonization). Furthermore, in the model we can specify persistence and
colonization probabilities as functions of covariates. Using our little
butterfly as an example, instead of assuming that the butterfly is more
likely to live in a larger meadow, we now assume that when the butterfly
lives in a meadow, it is more likely to continue living there the next
year if the meadow is larger, and when the butterfly does not live in a
meadow, they are more likely to move into that meadow next year if the
meadow is larger, and vice versa.
:::

## Where to from here

-   Static occupancy models consider neither space nor time

-   Dynamic occupancy models consider the temporal aspect but not
    spatial dependence between sites

-   Co-occurrence models

::: notes
Today we gradually add to the realism of these ecological models, we
address both temporal and spatial aspect of population status, but also
include species co-occurrence models.

The dynamic occupancy model I showed you only allows the parameters,
persistence, and colonization, to be functions of local environmental
covariates but not occupancy status at other sites.

In that sense, the dynamic occupancy model is non-spatial because the
occupancy dynamics at a given site are unrelated to that at any other
site, making the spatial configuration of the sites irrelevant.

This is obviously unrealistic and misses something very important, as we
have learned from all those metapopulation studies that population
dynamics at a site are driven not only by the environmental conditions
of that given site but also the connectivity (i.e., probability of
moving) between that site and other sites (Hanski 1998). For instance,
one might imagine that a site nearer an occupied site may have a higher
probability of being occupied than one that is further away, simply
because the potential of exchanging animals from the nearer site is
higher. Therefore, spatial dynamic occupancy models have been developed
to account for connectivity among sites.
:::

# 2.1 Spatial Dynamic Occupancy Models

## Spatial component

-   **Non-Spatial Limitation**: classic dynamic occupancy assumes
    colonization $\gamma_{it}$ is independent of occupancy at
    neighboring sites.
-   **Spatial Autocorrelation in Dynamics**:
    -   A site near occupied sites has a higher colonization
        probability.
-   **Spatial Colonization Model**:
    $$z_{i,1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_{i,1})$$
    $$z_{i,t} | z_{i,t-1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left( z_{i,t-1} \phi_{i,t-1} + (1 - z_{i,t-1}) \gamma_{i,t-1} \right)$$
    $$\gamma_{i,t-1} = f\left( \mathbf{X}_i, \text{Connectivity}(i, \mathbf{z}_{t-1}) \right)$$

::: notes
Transition from non-spatial dynamic occupancy to spatially explicit
dynamic occupancy models. Colonization at a site is related to the
occupancy status at other sites based on their connectivity with this
site. The simplest way of specifying connectivity is to assume that only
adjacent sites (also called neighbors) are connected.

The difference is the spatial dynamic occupancy model assumes that
colonization at an unoccupied site, γi, t - 1, is influenced by the
occupancy status of other sites given the connectivity between these
sites; the connectivity can further be a function of adjacency or
distance between these sites as well as environmental conditions in
these sites. The first part of the process sub-model of spatial dynamic
occupancy models describes the initial occupancy status of a species as
a function of covariates such z_i1 and psi_i1 the same as before.

The second part of the process sub-model describes the inter-annual
transitions of occupancy status, and again assumes that occupancy after
the first year is driven by persistence and colonization, and
persistence is a function of covariates

Spatial dynamic occupancy models also have an observation sub-model that
links detection/non-detection data to the true occupancy status given
some observation covariates.
:::

## Autologistic model: Logit-linear

Colonization/persistence at site *i* is a function of site *i*'s
neighborhood, i.e., how much of site *i*'s neighbourhood was occupied
last year.

-   **Logit-linear Autocovariate**: $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \color{#0d5f55}{A_{i,t-1}} &\color{#0d5f55}{= \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j \sim i} z_{j,t-1}}
    && \text{}\\[6pt]
    \text{logit}(\gamma_{i,t-1}) &= a^{\gamma}_0 + a^{\gamma}_1 x_i + \color{#0d5f55}{b^{\gamma}\, A_{i,t-1}}\\[6pt]
    \end{aligned}
    $$

$n_i$: Number of neighbours of site $i$ (3, 5 or 8 on a square grid with
a queen's neighbourhood).

$A_{i,t-1}$: The *proportion* of site $i$'s neighbours that were
occupied in year $t-1$.

$b^{\gamma}$: Effect of that local density on colonisation, on the logit
scale. Positive $b^{\gamma}$ is the signature of distance-limited
spread.

$a^{\gamma}_0$ : Baseline colonisation when no neighbours are occupied —
i.e. long-distance colonisation from outside the neighbourhood.

::: notes
$A_{i,t-1}$ is a covariate like any other, with one crucial difference:
**it is a function of the latent state**. You do not observe it; the
model estimates it. AHM2 is pointed about this. Some authors plug in the
*observed* proportion of occupied neighbours, which is biased by
imperfect detection.

$j \sim i$: $j$ is a neighbour of $i$, under whatever neighbourhood you
defined. $n_i$: Number of neighbours of site $i$ (3, 5 or 8 on a square
grid with a queen's neighbourhood). $A_{i,t-1}$: The **autocovariate**:
the *proportion* of site $i$'s neighbours that were occupied in year
$t-1$. Bounded in $[0,1]$. Read it as "the local density of potential
colonists — or rescuers — around site $i$." $b^{\gamma}$: Effect of that
local density on colonisation, on the logit scale. Positive $b^{\gamma}$
is the signature of distance-limited spread. $b^{\phi}$: Effect on
persistence. Positive $b^{\phi}$ is the **rescue effect**: a population
near other occupied sites is less likely to blink out, because
immigrants keep topping it up. $a^{\gamma}_0$ : Baseline colonisation
when no neighbours are occupied — i.e. long-distance colonisation from
outside the neighbourhood.

Computing the autocovariate from $z$ inside the model is the entire
point.

The neighbourhood size is a modelling choice that should reflect the
species' dispersal distance. AHM2 suggests trying several and inferring
dispersal from the one that fits best, or that yields the strongest
autocovariate effects.

The initial state, and the state transitions, and the observation
submodel are the same as nonspatial. For a continuous habitat, adjacency
can be defined as the case where two sites (polygons) share some of
their boundaries. For a patchy habitat such as the one we consider in
this book, adjacency can be defined as the case where two sites are
within a given distance. When adjacency is defined, the model assumes
that an unoccupied site can be colonized only if any of its adjacent
sites are occupied, and the probability of colonization is higher when
more of its adjacent sites are occupied.

AHM2 is explicit that the two mechanisms producing spatial
autocorrelation — an omitted spatially structured covariate, and a
biotic process like dispersal — "can yield exactly the same spatial
patterns," so you cannot normally tell them apart from a static pattern.
What you *can* do is write down a model whose parameters mean what you
want them to mean, and be clear about which you chose.
:::

## Autologistic model: adjacency indicator

-   **Autologistic Transition Form**: $$
    \gamma_{i,t-1} \;=\; 1 \;-\; \big(1-\zeta\big)^{\textstyle\sum_{i'} a_{i,i'}\, z_{i',t-1}} \times \big(1-\delta\big)
    $$ $a_{i,i'}$: Binary adjacency indicator, 1 if sites $i$ and $i'$
    are adjacent, 0 otherwise.

$\zeta$: Probability of colonisation contributed by **one** occupied
neighbour.

$\delta$: Probability of colonisation from **non-adjacent** sites
(long-distance movement)

::: notes
Read it as a failure-to-colonise product. Each occupied neighbour
independently fails to colonise site $i$ with probability $1-\zeta$; $k$
occupied neighbours all fail with probability $(1-\zeta)^k$;

long-distance colonisation independently fails with probability
$1-\delta$. One minus the product of all those failures is the
probability that *something* succeeded.

$a_{i,i'}$: Binary adjacency indicator, 1 if sites $i$ and $i'$ are
adjacent, 0 otherwise.

$\sum_{i'} a_{i,i'} z_{i',t-1}$: The **count** of occupied adjacent
sites in year $t-1$ (not the proportion)

$\zeta$: Probability of colonisation contributed by **one** occupied
neighbour.

$\delta$: Probability of colonisation from **non-adjacent** sites
(long-distance movement)

This is better than Formulation A: - With zero occupied neighbours,
$\gamma = \delta$ exactly. The baseline is a named, interpretable
parameter rather than a logit intercept. - $\gamma$ is monotone
increasing in the number of occupied neighbours and automatically
bounded in $[0,1]$ — no link function needed.
:::

## Distance-Based Movement

-   The definition of adjacency can be arbitrary if sites are not
    naturally adjacent to each other in patchy habitats.

-   It may be an oversimplification to assume that only adjacent sites
    are connected.

-   More realistic to assume that connectivity between two sites is
    related to their distance, typically with a negative relationship.

::: notes
Imagine a butterfly population, if the species does not live in a meadow
in a year, it has a better chance to move into this meadow from a closer
meadow than from a more distant one if they live in both. At the end of
the day, whether the butterfly will move into a meadow or not depends on
the number of meadows they live in and the distance from these meadows
to the empty meadow.
:::

## Distance-Based Dispersal Kernels

-   **Standardized Connectivity Weight**: $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \color{#0d5f55}{\eta_{i,i'}} &\color{#0d5f55}{= \exp\!\left(-\kappa\, d_{i,i'}\right)}
     && \text{unstandardised colonisation rate}\\[6pt]
    \color{#0d5f55}{\theta_{i,i'}} &\color{#0d5f55}{= \frac{\eta_{i,i'}}{\sum_{i''=1}^{M}\eta_{i,i''}}}
     && \text{standardised colonisation rate}\\[6pt]
    \end{aligned}
    $$

$d_{i,i'}$: Distance between sites $i$ and $i'$. Note $d_{i,i} = 0$, so
a site contributes to itself with weight $\eta = 1$.

$\kappa$: **Decay parameter**. Large $\kappa$ means colonisation falls
off fast with distance — a poor disperser. $\kappa \to 0$ means every
site contributes equally and space stops mattering.

$\eta_{i,i'}$: Raw kernel weight, in $(0,1]$. Equals 1 at zero
distance.\
$\theta_{i,i'}$: Kernel weight normalised so that
$\sum_{i'} \theta_{i,i'} = 1$ for every $i$.

$\gamma_{i,t-1}$: Colonisation probability — a **weighted average of the
occupancy states**, with weights that decay with distance.

-   **Colonization Probability**:
    $$\gamma_{i, t-1} = \sum_{i'=1}^{M} \theta_{i,i'}\, z_{i',t-1}$$

::: notes
The neighbourhood disappears. Instead of a sharp cutoff — in or out —
every site in the landscape contributes to the colonisation of every
other site, weighted by a **dispersal kernel** that decays with
distance.

To specify the relationship between colonization probability and
distance, we often use something called a decay function, i.e., a
monotone declining function of distance. Here we use a simple and widely
used decay function, which is

in which θi1,i2 is a parameter representing (standardized) colonization
rate between sites i1 and i2, ηi1,i2 is unstandardized colonization
rate, and κ is a decay parameter governing the relationship between
colonization and distance, denoted di1,i2 . A larger κ represents a more
rapid rate of decay, meaning that the colonization rate decreases faster
with increasing distance, and vice versa

The normalisation is doing elegant work. Because each row of
$\boldsymbol{\theta}$ sums to one, $\gamma_{i,t-1}$ is a convex
combination of zeros and ones and therefore lies in $[0,1]$
automatically. No link function, no risk of an invalid probability. Read
it as: *the colonisation probability of site* $i$ is the
distance-weighted proportion of the landscape that was occupied.
:::

## Combined Distance- and Environment-Based Movement

-   Dispersal depends on both geographic distance $d_{i,i'}$ AND habitat
    quality at source/target sites:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\color{#0d5f55}{\gamma_{i,t-1}} &\color{#0d5f55}{=
\underbrace{\text{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\beta^{[\gamma]}_0 + \beta^{[\gamma]}_1 x_{i,t,1} + \dots\right)}_{\text{local suitability}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i'=1}^{M}\theta_{i,i'}\, z_{i',t-1}}_{\text{connectivity}}}\\[8pt]
\theta_{i,i'} &= \frac{\eta_{i,i'}}{\sum_{i''}\eta_{i,i''}}, \qquad
\eta_{i,i'} = \exp(-\kappa\, d_{i,i'})
\end{aligned}
$$ **Local suitability**: how good a destination site $i$ is, given its
own covariates.

**Connectivity**: how much occupied habitat is within dispersal reach.

::: notes
More realistically, ... (Sutherland et al. 2012; Drake et al. 2022).
Imagine an area with just three meadows, where our butterfly lives in
one of them but not the other two. Also, imagine that the two empty
meadows are equally far from the meadow that the species live in, but
one empty meadow is much larger than the other. Based on the model
introduced in Sect. 2.4.2, the chance that the butterfly will move into
either of these empty meadows is the same. However, here we want to
consider the case when the butterfly is more likely to move into the
larger empty meadow.

with initial occupancy, persistence and the observation sub-model
exactly as in Module 6.

**Local suitability**: how good a destination site $i$ is, given its own
covariates. In $(0,1)$. **Connectivity**: how much occupied habitat is
within dispersal reach. In $[0,1]$ by the row-normalisation.

Both factors lie in $(0,1)$, so their product does too. Colonisation
requires *both* that colonists arrive *and* that the destination is
habitable.

The multiplicative form encodes a genuine ecological claim: **arrival
and establishment are separate events, and both must succeed.** A
perfectly suitable site that nothing can reach is not colonised
($\text{connectivity} \approx 0$). A site surrounded by occupied habitat
but hostile is not colonised either ($\text{suitability} \approx 0$).
That is more than a modelling convenience — it is the distinction
between dispersal limitation and habitat limitation, and this model lets
you estimate which one is binding.
:::

# 2.2 Spatial Co-occurrence Model

## Co-occurrence

Coexistence of interacting species has long been a focus in
metapopulation studies (Hanski and Gilpin 1997; Hanski 1998)

-   Occupancy status of a species is influenced by its abiotic
    environment and the presence or absence of other interacting
    species.

-   Species colonization/persistence is influenced by its abiotic
    environment and the presence or absence of other interacting
    species.

::: notes
Understanding the coexistence of interacting species has long been a
focus in metapopulation studies.

In this case, the occupancy status of a species is influenced not only
by its abiotic environment but also by the presence or absence of other
interacting species.

For example, competition and predator–prey interactions can influence
persistence and colonization, and thus the stability of local
populations (Bengtsson 1989; Bonsall et al. 2002). The capability of
moving among habitat patches is also key for metapopulation stability
:::

## Spatial Dynamic Co-occurrence Model

-   **Interspecific Interactions**: Modeling co-occurrence dynamics of
    species $s \in \{1, \dots, S\}$.
-   **Latent States**: $z_{i,t,s} \in \{0, 1\}$ for species $s$ at site
    $i$, year $t$.
-   **Interaction Mechanisms**:
    -   Predator presence ($z_{i,t-1, \text{pred}} = 1$) reduces prey
        persistence $\phi_{i,t-1,\text{prey}}$ and colonization
        $\gamma_{i,t-1,\text{prey}}$.
    -   Prey presence increases predator persistence and colonization.

::: notes
Multispecies extension incorporates competitive or predator-prey state
dependencies.
:::

## Predator-Prey Prsistence

-   **Prey Persistence**:
    $$\text{logit}(\phi_{i,t-1,\text{prey}}) = \beta_0^{(\phi,\text{prey})} + \beta_{\text{pred}}^{(\phi,\text{prey})} \times z_{i,t-1,\text{pred}} + \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}$$
-   **Predator Persistence**:
    $$\text{logit}(\phi_{i,t-1,\text{pred}}) = \beta_0^{(\phi,\text{pred})} + \beta_{\text{prey}}^{(\phi,\text{pred})} \times z_{i,t-1,\text{prey}} + \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}$$
-   Expected Signs: $\beta_{\text{pred}}^{(\phi,\text{prey})} < 0$ (prey
    suppressed) and $\beta_{\text{prey}}^{(\phi,\text{pred})} > 0$
    (predator supported).

::: notes
Equations governing interspecific state-dependent turnover.
:::

## Case Study: Ant vs Butterfly Meadow Metapopulation

-   **System**: Invasive ant (*Myrmica*) vs native lycaenid butterfly.
-   **Hypothesis**: Ant presence induces local extinction of butterfly
    caterpillar patches.
-   **Dynamic Occupancy Estimates**:
    -   Butterfly persistence $\phi_{\text{butterfly}}$ drops from
        $0.85$ (ant absent) to $0.22$ (ant present).
    -   Butterfly colonization $\gamma_{\text{butterfly}}$ reduced by
        $65\%$ in ant-dominated meadows.

::: notes
Empirical illustration of competitive exclusion in dynamic occupancy.
:::

::: notes
Here, we consider a model in which persistence and colonization of one
species are functions of abiotic environmental covariates as well as
occupancy of other species. For illustration, imagine that our little
butterfly lives in the same area as some ant species that is a fierce
predator of the butterfly. If the butterfly lives in a meadow, it will
be less likely to continue living there if the ant also lives in the
same meadow (because all of the butterflies may simply be eaten!).
Conversely, if the ant lives in a meadow, it will be more likely to
continue living there if the butterfly is there (because the ant gets to
eat the butterfly). Meanwhile, we can also imagine that the butterfly is
less likely to move into a meadow where the ant lives in, and the ant is
more likely to move into a meadow if the butterfly is there. Using
statistical language, we have the following for the first year: in which
zi, 1, s is the occupancy status of species s at site i and year 1, ψi,
1, s is the initial occupancy probability, and β ½ \] 0 ∙ ,s’s are
species-specific intercepts and slopes governing the effects of
covariates (x’s) on initial occupancy. Here, if we consider a system
with two species (i.e., nspec = 2), we will have s = ant or butterfly.
From the second year, we have
:::

# 3.1 Simulations

## Simulate the orchid network

![](images/orchid.jpg){width="40%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 6.4
#| echo: true
set.seed(1010)
n_p <- 841                        # patches

# patches scatter along a sinuous river channel, in metres
tt <- sort(runif(n_p, 0, 1))
rx <- 300 * tt + rnorm(n_p, 0, 6)
ry <- -300 * tt + 40 * sin(8 * tt) + rnorm(n_p, 0, 6)
rz <- 60 * tt + rnorm(n_p, 0, 2)          # elevation gradient along the river

area <- round(rlnorm(n_p, log(35), 1.0), 1)     # moss area, cm2
area <- pmin(area, 650)

# 3-D distance
dmat <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(rx, ry, rz)))

meandist <- 4.8             # mean seed dispersal, m (Tremblay 1997)
alpha <- 1 / meandist

plot(rx, 
     ry,
     pch = 21,
     bg = "grey85",
     cex = log(area + 1) / 3,
     xlab = "x (m)", 
     ylab = "y (m)", 
     asp = 1,
     main = "841 moss patches along the river; symbol size ~ log(area)")
c(patches = n_p,
  mean_area = round(mean(area), 1),
  max_area = max(area), 
  alpha = round(alpha, 3))
```

::: notes
Lepanthes rupestris is a small wind-dispersed orchid, leaves 1.3 to 4.3
cm, flowers under 6 mm, that anchors its roots in moss patches on
boulders (epilithic) or tree trunks (epiphytic) along streams in the
Luquillo Mountains, Puerto Rico. Rocks tend to have larger populations
and higher occupancy than trees.

The sampling design is worth noting for its cleverness. 250 occupied
patches were identified first, then unoccupied patches were found by
randomly selecting three suitable moss-covered patches with no
individuals within a 5 m radius of each occupied patch. That gives you
unoccupied patches that are genuinely SUITABLE, which is what you need
to estimate colonization.

Note the THREE-DIMENSIONAL distance. The patches sit along a steep
elevation gradient, and dist() takes x, y and z without complaint. Most
connectivity work ignores the vertical dimension; along a mountain
stream that is a real omission.

Mean seed dispersal is 4.8 m, so alpha is about 0.21 -- a severely
dispersal- limited organism, which is exactly why the metapopulation
framing fits.
:::

## Simulate occupancy dynamics

```{r}
#| echo: true
# TRUTH
b_psi   <- c(int = -2.899, area = 0.562, S = 0.185)
b_eps   <- c(int = -1.21,  area = -0.62)
logit_g <- -4.14                       # colonization, constant
p_det   <- 0.843                       # per-survey detection

n_prim <- 5; n_sec <- 2
logarea <- log(area + 1)

# connectivity S_i, ignoring occupancy 
gker <- exp(-alpha * dmat); diag(gker) <- 0
S <- as.vector(gker %*% area)
Sz <- as.numeric(scale(S))             # centres and scales S

psi1 <- plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * logarea + b_psi["S"] * Sz)
eps  <- plogis(b_eps["int"] + b_eps["area"] * logarea)
gam  <- plogis(logit_g)

set.seed(1011)
z <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_p, n_prim)
z[, 1] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, psi1)
for (t in 2:n_prim) {
  pr <- z[, t - 1] * (1 - eps) + (1 - z[, t - 1]) * gam
  z[, t] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, pr)
}

# observation: two secondary surveys per primary period
y <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_p, n_prim * n_sec)
for (t in 1:n_prim) for (j in 1:n_sec) {
  y[, (t - 1) * n_sec + j] <- rbinom(n_p, 1, z[, t] * p_det)
}

# Counts as well as occupancy: holds abundance N, and
# the synchrony analysis needs a series with variance. A purely binary series
# from a patch that never changes state has sd = 0.
lamN <- exp(0.4 + 0.35 * logarea)          # expected count when occupied
N <- matrix(0L, n_p, n_prim)
for (t in 1:n_prim) N[, t] <- as.integer(z[, t] * rpois(n_p, lamN))

c(ever_occupied_true = sum(rowSums(z) > 0),
  ever_detected = sum(rowSums(y) > 0),
  detections = sum(y), non_detections = sum(y == 0),
  detection_rate = round(mean(y), 3),
  psi_star_expected = round(mean(gam / (gam + eps)), 3),
  mean_count_when_occupied = round(mean(N[z == 1]), 1))
```

::: notes
Everything here is generated from the book's own estimates, so Lab D can
be scored against a known truth.

Check the printed numbers against theirs. They report 1969 detections
and 6641 non-detections, a detection rate of 0.229, 266 patches ever
occupied, and an equilibrium psi\* of 0.31. Ours should be in the same
neighbourhood.

Two things worth pointing at in the loop. The transition line

pr \<- z\[, t-1\] \* (1 - eps) + (1 - z\[, t-1\]) \* gam

IS equation 10.19 -- the switch we discussed. And note
EVER_OCCUPIED_TRUE versus EVER_DETECTED: the gap is the patches that
were occupied and never detected. With p = 0.843 and ten surveys that
gap should be tiny, which is why the book's detection correction changes
little here.

Note also colonization is CONSTANT while extinction depends on area.
That is the book's best-supported model, and it means the area-isolation
paradigm only half holds in this system -- area drives extinction,
isolation does not measurably drive colonization.
:::

```{r}
library(unmarked)
site_cov <- data.frame(logarea = logarea, Sz = Sz)

# a survey-level covariate: day of year, standardised
set.seed(1012)
date_mat <- matrix(scale(as.vector(
  outer(rep(1, n_p), rep(c(40, 210), n_prim)) + rnorm(n_p * n_prim * n_sec, 0, 8)
))[, 1], n_p, n_prim * n_sec)

# implicit-dynamics frame: stack primary periods as if independent
y_stack   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n_prim,
                     function(t) y[, (t - 1) * n_sec + 1:n_sec]))
cov_stack <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_prim, site_cov, simplify = FALSE))
dat_stack <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n_prim,
                     function(t) date_mat[, (t - 1) * n_sec + 1:n_sec]))

umf_occ <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y_stack, siteCovs = cov_stack,
                             obsCovs = list(date = dat_stack))

# dynamic frame: all 10 surveys, 5 primary periods
umf_dyn <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = y, siteCovs = site_cov,
                             obsCovs = list(date = date_mat),
                             numPrimary = n_prim)
c(stacked_rows = nrow(y_stack), dynamic_sites = numSites(umf_dyn))
```

::: notes
Two frames because we fit two kinds of model.

The IMPLICIT-DYNAMICS frame stacks the five primary periods on top of
each other and treats them as independent sites. That estimates AVERAGE
occupancy over time and ignores colonization and extinction entirely.
The book does this first and is explicit about the compromise: this is
repeated measures treated as independent samples, and unmarked cannot
easily fit random effects, so proceed with caution. Bayesian approaches
handle it properly (Rota et al. 2011).

The DYNAMIC frame keeps the structure: 841 sites, 10 surveys, 5 primary
periods. numPrimary is what tells unmarked where the primary boundaries
are.

On reshaping: real data arrive long, and you would reshape with
reshape2::dcast or base R. The base equivalent is one line --
xtabs(presence \~ siteID + survey_number, data = surveys) -- which is
worth knowing since reshape2 is superseded.
:::

# 3.2 Fit occupancy models

## First, ignore the dynamics

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: true
m_p_null <- occu(~ 1 ~ 1, umf_occ)
m_p_date <- occu(~ date ~ 1, umf_occ)
m_p_both <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ 1, umf_occ)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("p(.)" = m_p_null, 
                           "p(date)" = m_p_date,
                           "p(date+area)" = m_p_both)))
```

::: notes
The implicit-dynamics approach: estimate AVERAGE occupancy over the five
years and ignore colonization and extinction.

The formula syntax is unmarked's and catches people out: the FIRST tilde
is the DETECTION model, the SECOND is occupancy. So `occu(~ date ~ 1)`
means detection varies with date, occupancy is constant.

We fit the detection model first, holding occupancy constant, which is
the book's sequence. Note fitList(fits = list(...)) rather than
fitList("name" = model, ...) -- both work, but the explicit form is
unambiguous.

Our simulation has CONSTANT detection, so date and area should NOT
improve the model. The book's real data strongly supported both. That
difference is honest: their detection genuinely varied, ours does not by
construction.
:::

## Now add area and isolation

```{r}
#| echo: true

m_area   <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ logarea, umf_occ)
m_S      <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ Sz, umf_occ)
m_areaS  <- occu(~ date + logarea ~ logarea + Sz, umf_occ)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("psi(.)" = m_p_both,
                           "psi(area)" = m_area,
                           "psi(S)" = m_S, 
                           "psi(area+S)" = m_areaS)))
round(coef(m_areaS), 3)
```

::: notes
Now covariates on occupancy. The book's most-supported model is area +
S, with both effects positive: as patch area and connectivity increase,
occupancy increases. Their estimates are intercept -2.899, area 0.562, S
0.185, and the z-value for area is much larger, so the area effect is
stronger.

Compare our estimates to those numbers -- they are the truth we
simulated from.

One subtle point the book makes well, and it is worth repeating. When
they fitted detection alone, patch area appeared to strongly affect
DETECTABILITY. Once area was also in the occupancy model, the detection
effect shrank a lot. Their explanation: covariate effects on detection
and occupancy are not formally confounded, but the model does use shared
information during estimation. So be careful interpreting a covariate
that plausibly affects both.

Ours will show this less dramatically, because we simulated constant
detection.
:::

## Colonization and extinction, explicitly

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: true

m_dyn_null <- colext(psiformula = ~ 1,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ 1,
                     pformula = ~ 1, 
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_psi  <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ 1, 
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_eps  <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ 1,
                     epsilonformula = ~ logarea, 
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

m_dyn_full <- colext(psiformula = ~ logarea + Sz,
                     gammaformula = ~ Sz,
                     epsilonformula = ~ logarea,
                     pformula = ~ 1,
                     data = umf_dyn)

modSel(fitList(fits = list("null" = m_dyn_null,
                           "psi(area+S)" = m_dyn_psi,
                           "psi(area+S) eps(area)" = m_dyn_eps,
                           "+ gamma(S)"           = m_dyn_full)))
```

::: notes
Four models of increasing complexity. Note colext() takes FOUR formulas:
initial occupancy, colonization (gamma), extinction (epsilon), and
detection.

The book's model ranking puts psi(area+S) with eps(area) on top, with
gamma(S) adding nothing -- delta AIC of 1.6, so within noise. Their
conclusion: patch area has a strong NEGATIVE effect on extinction, and
connectivity S is NOT a strong predictor of colonization.

That is a partial failure of the area-isolation paradigm in this system,
and it is worth dwelling on. Area does what the theory says. Isolation
does not. The book is straightforward about it rather than reaching for
an explanation.

Our simulation has constant colonization by construction, so the
gamma(S) model should also add nothing. Good -- that means the model
selection is behaving.

colext() is the slowest thing in this deck: it evaluates a two-state
hidden Markov likelihood over 841 sites and 5 periods for every optim
step.
:::

## Did it recover the truth?

```{r}
#| echo: true
est <- coef(m_dyn_eps)

# coef() for a colext fit returns psi, then col, then ext, then det. This
# vector is in that order -- READ THE PRINTED NAMES to confirm rather than
# trusting the order, and the stopifnot catches a length mismatch.
truth_vec <- c(b_psi[["int"]], 
               b_psi[["area"]],
               b_psi[["S"]],   # psi
               logit_g,          # col
               b_eps[["int"]], 
               b_eps[["area"]],  # ext
               qlogis(p_det))     # det
stopifnot(length(est) == length(truth_vec))

data.frame(parameter  = names(est),
           estimate   = round(as.numeric(est), 3),
           truth      = round(truth_vec, 3),
           difference = round(as.numeric(est) - truth_vec, 3))

round(c(gamma = backTransform(m_dyn_eps, type = "col")@estimate,
        p     = backTransform(m_dyn_eps, type = "det")@estimate), 4)
```

::: notes
Seven parameters, side by side with the values that generated the data.

Expect the psi and extinction coefficients to be close. The colonization
intercept may be noisier, because colonization events are rare -- gamma
is about 0.016, so across 841 patches and four transitions you observe
relatively few. Rare events, wide confidence intervals.

backTransform() converts from the logit scale to probabilities. Compare
gamma to 0.016 and p to 0.843.

Note the order of coef() output: initial occupancy, then colonization,
then extinction, then detection. If the truth vector and the estimate
vector were misaligned the differences would be nonsense, so read the
parameter names, do not trust the order.
:::

## Partial predictions

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 12.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
ar_seq <- seq(min(logarea), max(logarea), length.out = 60)
S_seq  <- seq(min(Sz), max(Sz), length.out = 60)

nd_area <- data.frame(logarea = ar_seq, Sz = mean(Sz))
nd_S    <- data.frame(logarea = mean(logarea), Sz = S_seq)

# NOTE: predict(object, type, newdata) -- name BOTH, the 2nd positional is type
pr_psi_a <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_area)
pr_psi_S <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_S)
pr_ext_a <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "ext", newdata = nd_area)

band <- function(x, p, xlab, ylab, main, truth = NULL) {
  plot(x, p$Predicted, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = main)
  lines(x, p$lower, lty = 2); lines(x, p$upper, lty = 2)
  if (!is.null(truth)) lines(x, truth, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2.4, lty = 3)
}

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
band(exp(ar_seq) - 1, pr_psi_a, "patch area (cm2)", "initial occupancy",
     "psi vs area",
     plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * ar_seq + b_psi["S"] * mean(Sz)))
band(S_seq, pr_psi_S, "connectivity S (scaled)", "", "psi vs S",
     plogis(b_psi["int"] + b_psi["area"] * mean(logarea) + b_psi["S"] * S_seq))
band(exp(ar_seq) - 1, pr_ext_a, "patch area (cm2)", "extinction",
     "extinction vs area",
     plogis(b_eps["int"] + b_eps["area"] * ar_seq))
par(op)
```

::: notes
extinction probability falls steeply with patch area. That is the area
half of the area-isolation paradigm, and it is well supported.

The book's summary of the comparison between the implicit and dynamic
models is worth repeating: the area effect on average occupancy was
driven PARTLY by extinction dynamics, and since area also explains
occupancy at time 1, dynamics before the surveys began -- before 2000 --
presumably contributed too.

That is a nice illustration of a general point. A snapshot of occupancy
encodes the accumulated history of colonization and extinction, and you
cannot separate them without time series.
:::

# 3.3 Project forward {.center}

## Project the fitted dynamics

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
nd_fit  <- data.frame(logarea = logarea, Sz = Sz)
psi_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "psi", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted
col_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "col", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted
ext_hat <- predict(m_dyn_eps, type = "ext", newdata = nd_fit)$Predicted

colext_sim <- function(psi0, col, ext, timeframe, reps) {
  ns <- length(psi0)
  out <- array(NA_integer_, dim = c(reps, ns, timeframe))
  out[, , 1] <- rbinom(reps * ns, 1, rep(psi0, each = reps))
  for (t in 2:timeframe) {
    prev <- out[, , t - 1]
    pr <- prev * (1 - rep(ext, each = reps)) +
          (1 - prev) * rep(col, each = reps)
    out[, , t] <- rbinom(reps * ns, 1, pr)
  }
  out
}

set.seed(1013)
proj <- colext_sim(psi_hat, col_hat, ext_hat, timeframe = 100, reps = 20)
land_mean <- apply(proj, c(1, 3), mean)          # reps x time

psi_star <- mean(col_hat / (col_hat + ext_hat))

op <- par(mar = c(4.4, 4.6, 3, 1))
matplot(t(land_mean), type = "l", lty = 1, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.25),
        ylim = c(0, 0.6), xlab = "time step",
        ylab = "proportion of patches occupied",
        main = "100-year projection, 20 realizations")
lines(colMeans(land_mean), lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = psi_star, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
text(80, psi_star + 0.03, expression(psi^"*"), col = "firebrick", cex = 1.3)
par(op)
round(c(psi_star = psi_star, projected_end = mean(land_mean[, 100])), 3)
```

::: notes
Twenty realizations of a 100-year projection, using patch-specific
colonization and extinction from the fitted model. Red dashed line is
the predicted equilibrium.

Now the apparent paradox the book raises, and it is the best teaching
moment in the chapter. Estimated extinction rates are HIGHER than
colonization rates -- gamma \< epsilon -- and yet the projection is
stable or rising. But the Levins model said persistence requires c \> e.
What gives?

Two reasons, and the second is the important one.

First, rates vary by patch, whereas Levins assumes they do not.

Second, and crucially, THE PARAMETERS ARE NOT THE SAME QUANTITY. In the
Levins model, c is the rate of individuals EMIGRATING from occupied
patches. In a dynamic occupancy model, gamma is the PROBABILITY THAT AN
EMPTY PATCH BECOMES COLONIZED in one primary period. Different units,
different meanings. Comparing them is a category error.

The right equilibrium for this model is psi\* = gamma / (gamma +
epsilon), and the projection should converge on it. Check the two
printed numbers.

Caveat the book flags: this projection ignores parameter uncertainty.
Propagating it properly needs a Bayesian treatment (Chandler et al.
2015).
:::
